daily.title: Why we still write letters
daily.author: Clare Whitfield
body: In the morning light of the Blackheath post office, Mrs Higgins still weighs parcels on brass scales that have outlived three postal ministers. There is something quietly stubborn about dropping an envelope into the red pillar box on the corner, the hollow thud as it falls into darkness.

We send messages across satellites in milliseconds now, yet none of them smell of cedar drawers or carry the hesitation of an inked cross-out. A handwritten note asks you to sit still with one person in your mind, holding their silence alongside your own.
QUOTE:A letter is a small promise that someone will still be there when it arrives.
So I keep a box of good paper in the drawer by the kettle. Once a week, while the water boils, I write to someone. Most of them write back.

daily.title: The town that gold built
daily.author: Clare Whitfield
body: Bendigo wears its fortune on its facades: wrought iron lace, sandstone banks and a fountain nobody quite knows what to do with.

reference.title: Victorian Gold Rush
reference.summary: How the 1851 discoveries turned a pastoral colony into a boom economy.
body: Gold was found near Clunes and then at Ballarat in the winter of 1851. Within months, shepherds, clerks and sailors had walked off the job, and ships sat empty in Port Phillip Bay while their crews headed for the diggings.
The colony's population grew sevenfold in a decade. Licence fees, tent cities and boomtown architecture followed, along with the tensions that would end at the Eureka Stockade in 1854.

reference.title: Eureka Stockade
reference.summary: The miners' rebellion over licence fees at Ballarat.
body: On 3 December 1854 soldiers stormed a hastily built stockade on the Eureka lead.
